paragraphs: Rabbi Abba Sedronya, Rabbah, Naso, section 14. Mattenot Kehunah explains it as a place name. In my opinion this is the one mentioned in Midrash Rabbah, end of Mattot: “What does ‘not from the wilderness of mountains’ mean? Rabbi Abba of Romanya said: Everywhere Scripture says harim it means mountains, except here, ‘not from the wilderness harim,’ where it means exaltation.” Yedei Moshe explains: “Of Romanya means of the mountains, an expression of exaltation, as it concludes that a person does not rise through these things.” End quotation. Thus he interprets meromanya as exaltation. In my opinion he has departed from the plain meaning: Rabbi Abba was from a place called Romanya. Reliable testimony is that Yalkut, Mattot, and Psalms, section 75, lack the word meromanya; likewise the Arukh, entry har, and the Shorashim: “Every harim means mountains, except here.” They too understood it as a place name, and so did not bother copying meromanya. Kohelet Rabbah, on “The profit of the land is for all”: the old synagogue of Seronya. Bereshit Rabbah, section 1: Rabbi Abba Serongya. All are one; there is not a second, despite the varying forms Sedronya, Serongya, and meromanya. Such errors are common in Rabbah, particularly in personal and place names. “Rejoice, my innards: if over doubtful matters,” etc.; for after some time I indeed found and saw in Tanchuma, Mattot: “Rabbi Abba Sangorya said: Every harim in Scripture,” etc. Jerusalem Talmud, chapter Lulav Va'aravah: Rabbi Ba Serongyah expounded. Rabbah, Prague edition, year 384 [שפ״ד; millennium not stated]: Rabbi Abba Seronnya. Thus your eyes see that the author of Yedei Moshe departed from the plain meaning. (See Rabbi Bibi Margenya.)
